newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE - Pol Pot, a shadow in pages of Cambodia's history.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Pol Pot, a shadow in pages of Cambodia's history.

text.p: Khmer Rouge chief Pol Pot is one of the 20th century's most notorious figures, but young Cambodians could be forgiven for having just a hazy understanding of his 1975-79 rule.
The Khmer Rouge reign of terror that left more than one million people dead is covered in just a few short paragraphs in Cambodia's high school history books.
At Phnom Penh University, it's the topic of just two or three classes in a four-year programme.
And in primary school, Pol Pot and his "killing fields" regime are not mentioned at all.
Pol Pot, an enigma to the journalists and political leaders who hoped in vain to see him emerge from the northern jungle in recent weeks, is also proving to be a mystery to Cambodia's students.
The reason, say educators, is the Khmer Rouge era is too terrible, too painful and still too politically sensitive for the history books.
THE PERIOD SEEN STILL TOO CONTROVERSIAL
"I am angry with Pol Pot but it is not necessary to repeat the facts over and over. It is not useful," says In Kim Srun, chief editor at the Education Ministry's textbook department.

"At the primary level, we don't want young children to remember the facts. But for high school, we have some description but no commentary. We don't want the students to have to know everything," he told Reuters in an interview.
Other educators say the period is still too controversial to teach. Many members of the current government were former members of the Khmer Rouge who split with Pol Pot during his rule.

Other members of the government were for a period linked with the Khmer Rouge in a coalition government-in-exile, which fought a Vietnamese army of occupation and the Hanoi-backed government through the 1980s.
Delving deeply into the history of the Khmer Rouge era would only divide the already politically troubled country, the educators said.
The result is that Cambodia's youth -- half the population -- get very little formal education about the darkest chapter in the country's modern history.
FOR HALF POPULATION, POL POT YEARS ARE HISTORY
During Pol Pot's disastrous four-year experiment with extreme communism, almost the entire population was forced into rural work camps and decimated by execution, disease, starvation and exhaustion.

The Khmer Rouge were ousted from power by a Vietnamese invasion in 1979 and then waged war from the country's jungles. The group has been seriously weakened by defections and a recent split among top leaders which resulted in Pol Pot's removal as supreme leader.
For many adult Cambodians, Pol Pot's rule is a nightmare they can never forget. But for the country's youth, it is history.
"This story finished 18 years ago, and half the population is less than 18 years old," said Cambodia expert Raoul Jennar, author of the "Keys to Cambodia."
In Kim Srun said his 18-year-old son hardly believes what he is told about the Pol Pot period, even though the boy lost eight of his 10 aunts and uncles and an older brother he never knew.
LACK OF TEACHING MATERIALS
It is a problem that is compounded by a dearth of academic materials for students, said Sorn Samnang, chairman of Phnom Penh University's history department.

While foreign scholars have written volumes on the period, virtually none has been translated into the Cambodian language. The cash-strapped history faculty is hard-pressed to start producing new books from scratch, Sorn Samnang said.
"It's not really taught, because we don't have enough of a chance to prepare lessons," he told Reuters.
It hasn't always been that way.
In the 1980s, school books contained lessons on the Khmer Rouge, but the material, printed by the Hanoi-backed regime that ruled at the time, was too politically biased, educators say.
Now they are reluctant to pass their own judgment on the time and risk upsetting politicians or stirring up old memories, they said.

Many Cambodians and foreigners say an international tribunal should be set up to force Pol Pot and other guerrilla leaders to answer for their crimes and set the record straight once and for all. Judgment should be passed in a courtroom, not the class room, they said.
"(Cambodians) need to turn the page -- but without ignoring the past," Jennar said.
